new_statements.quote: Sedangkan bahasa-bahasa yang dikelompokkan ke dalam keluarga bahasa Geelvink Bay adalah bahasa-bahasa Papua yang berada di wilayah bagian barat dari daratan Mamberamo ke wilayah Waropen, dan beberapa bagian di wilayah Nabire dan Pulau Yapen. Bahasa-bahasa seperti bahasa Kirikiri, Demisa, Fayu, Iau, Biritai, Burate, Awera, Tarunggare, Onate, dan lain-lain masuk dalam keluarga bahasa ini. [...] Bahasa-bahasa ini hampir merupakan bahasa bunyi (tonal languages) yang sistem morfologinya tidak serumit bahasa-bahasa Trans New Guinea, tetapi mempunyai sistem fonologi suprasegmetal yang sangat rumit, yaitu sistem bunyi (tone)nya berkisar antara 3 sampai 9 tone.
new_statements.translation: The languages grouped into the Geelvink Bay family are Papuan languages located in the area from the west of the Mamberamo mainland to the Waropen area, and some parts of the Nabire area and Yapen Island. Languages such as Kirikiri, Demisa, Fayu, Iau, Biritai, Burate, Awera, Tarunggare, Onate and others belong to this family. [...] These languages are almost [all] tone languages (tonal languages), whose morphology is not as complex as that of the Trans New Guinea languages, but which have a very complex suprasegmental phonology, namely tone systems ranging from 3 to 9 tones.

Nothing specific to Tunggare, hedged ('hampir'), and third-hand in a typological overview. | checker: Crossref record for doi 10.26499/li.v36i2.79 (downloaded via reader gate) confirms Sawaki, 'Meneropong tipologi bahasa-bahasa di Papua: suatu tinjuan singkat', Linguistik Indonesia 36(2): 129-143, open viewFile link at ojs.linguistik-indonesia.org. new_statements.relation_note: States that the group containing Tarunggare consists 'almost' entirely of tonal languages with 3-9 tones (pp.131-2) and, for Papua generally, that word stress is usually penultimate or final (p.133); nothing specific to Tarunggare/Wate, whose only data anywhere are untoned wordlists.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level claim: the 'Geelvink Bay' languages (list including Tarunggare) are 'almost' all tonal with 3-9 tones; no Tarunggare-specific statement, no statement on Tarunggare stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Names 'Tarunggare' (= Tunggare/Wate, trt) explicitly, p.131, as a member of Sawaki's 'Geelvink Bay' family located 'west of the Mamberamo to Waropen, parts of Nabire and Yapen'; but that group as he assembles it mixes Lakes Plain languages (Kirikiri, Fayu, Iau, Biritai/Obokuitai, Awera) with East Geelvink Bay ones (Demisa, Burate, Tarunggare), and the prosodic claim is made for the group as a whole, not from any Tarunggare data (none exist: Voorhoeve 1975, Kamholz 2012). Author: Universitas Papua / CELD Manokwari; a typological overview in Indonesian, third-hand for this language.

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2012. The Keuw isolate: preliminary materials and classification. In Harald Hammarstrom & Wilco van den Heuvel (eds.), History, contact and classification of Papuan languages (Language & Linguistics in Melanesia Special Issue 2012, Part I), 243-268. sources.note: Nothing for Wate/Tunggare. The Wate material is 18 untoned, unstressed forms (arm neʔeha, bone ha, breast roa, ear uro.. two amaite, urine wuo) used to show Keuw is unrelated, plus the remark that Wate/Tarunggare is mutually intelligible with Burate. All prosodic statements in the paper ('Keuw evidently has lexically contrastive tone', p. 249; 'has at least two tones', abstract) concern Keuw, not Wate. Useful pointer: note 6 documents that Kamholz holds unpublished Wate field notes (2008, 2011).
